newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria troops said to have killed GIA chief.
newsitem.headline: Algeria troops said to have killed GIA chief.

text.p: Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) chief Antar Zouabri, known as one of the country's most ruthless militants, has been killed by security forces in an ambush, sources close to the security services said on Thursday.
"He was killed last Tuesday with other members of the armed group," one of the sources said, adding that he died in a tunnel in Attatba region, between Tipaza and Blida, south of Algiers.
Zouabri, 27, is at least the eighth GIA chief to die since December 1992 when the group issued its first communique. One leader, Mansouri Meliani, was executed by firing squad in 1993.
Earlier on Thursday, Algerian newspapers said troops had trapped and may have killed Zouabri, who took over leadership of the ruthless Moslem fundamentalist group late last year.
The previous leader Jamal Zitouni died in a power struggle in July 1996, according to Algerian security sources.
Algiers blames the GIA for massacring hundreds of people. Most had their throats cut, including babies, young girls and women.

Last January, Zouabri, who comes from Boufarik 25 km (15 miles) south of Algiers, said in a statement: "There is no neutrality in the war we lead. Except for those who are with us, all the others are renegades."

There was no confirmation of Zouabri's death or any direct official comment on a huge military operation in which he was apparently caught and in which, according to Algerian newspapers, up to 140 rebels have been killed.
One influential newspaper, the Arabic-language Al Khabar, reported "some sources" as saying a mass grave with about 100 bodies had been found during the military operation.
It was discovered by troops advancing across rough terrain in an operation against the GIA rebels on the heights of Attatba.
"It is not known so far if these are the bodies of civilians or terrorists killed in the first days of the operation in the region where heads of the GIA were expected to meet," it said.

The start of the vast military operation coincided with the release earlier this month of Abassi Madani, president of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) who was halfway through a 12-year jail term for threatening state security.

Madani's FIS swept to a commanding lead in Algeria's first general election which the authorities cancelled in January 1992. Violence rapidly followed, with a FIS armed wing springing up and later the GIA forming.
About 60,000 people have been killed in the violence.
Algeria has since held its first multi-candidate presidential election, won by appointed incumbent Liamine Zeroual, and last month held a new parliamentary election.
Moderate Islamist parties were allowed to stand and two of them gained a total of 103 seats in the 380 member house.
One of the Islamist-leaning parties, the Movement of a Peaceful Society, has seven posts in the coalition government.
On Wednesday, Zeroual announced that local elections would be held on October 23, a final step in restoring elected institutions which crumbled amid the violence.
The authorities see restoration of elected bodies as a major step towards ending the crisis which has shaken the North African country of 29 million people.
Last month's general election brought no leltup in the violence. More than 400 civilians have been killed since then.

Just this week, Moslem rebels killed 47 people, mostly by cutting their throats, in two attacks south of Algiers, Le Matin daily newspaper said on Wednesday. Another newspaper El Watan said a total of 54 people had been killed.

On Thursday Liberte newspaper said the latest massacres seemed to be an attempt by other rebels groups to try to force the military to deploy away from Zouabri and his trapped men and give them chance to break out of the vice.
